newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO nervous at prospect of handling Boeing row.
newsitem.headline: WTO nervous at prospect of handling Boeing row.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) officials reacted cautiously on Friday to the prospect that the United States might bring the Boeing aircraft merger row with Brussels before the body for a ruling.

But trade analysts said Washington could have a case under WTO rules if the European Union decided to impose fines on European airlines accepting delivery of new planes from Boeing if it implements a merger with McDonnell Douglas.

"The U.S. and the EU are two of our biggest members. We hope they resolve this amicably and rapidly," the trade body's spokesman Keith Rockwell said when asked about a signal from U.S. President Bill Clinton that he could seek a WTO ruling.

Trade envoys in Geneva, headquarters of the two-and- a-half year old body, said a row of such complexity involving the world's top trading powers could tear at the fabric of its carefully nurtured dispute settlement procedure.

Not only could it bog down the system, currently handling nearly 70 cases, but with the emotional issues of jurisdiction and the vast sums of money involved an adverse outcome could tempt either side to brush aside any WTO ruling.

A similar challenge was avoided in 1995 when the United States and Japan settled a major row over automobiles. Another -- the EU-U.S. dispute over the Helms-Burton law on investment in Cuba -- is presently in suspense.

"I can understand that there is a degree of nervousness about this," said one diplomat. "Basically, everyone in Geneva would like the problem to go away -- or at least for the Americans and Europeans to solve it themselves."

Clinton, apparently speaking off the cuff during a photo session at the White House on Thursday, suggested Washington might take the WTO route, or impose unilateral sanctions, if the EU moved to block the merger.
"We have a system for managing this through the World Trade Organisation and we have some options ourselves when actions are taken by Europe in this regard," he said.

The WTO dispute settlement system, in whose shaping the United States played a major role, provides for final rulings by neutral panels and appeals boards within a maximum of 18 months of a complaint being formally lodged.

Throughout protracted negotiations with Boeing, the EU has argued that the merger would create a dominant global firm damaging fair competition in Europe. Brussels is expected to take a final decision on whether to block it on July 23.

The WTO has no specific rules on competition policy, although a committee looking into the area was set up after EU prodding by ministers from the body's currently 131 member countries at their Singapore conference last December.

However, the trade analysts said if Washington decided -- as some signs have suggested it might -- to argue that any fines Brussels imposed were effectively tariffs then it could challenge the EU under present WTO accords.

Under a 1979 agreement on trade in civil aircraft, some 20 trade powers including the United States and the then European Community agreed to abolish tariffs on all civil aircraft, engines and components.

Although that accord -- under the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) -- has not been incorporated into the WTO, the EU committed itself under the 1994 treaty setting up the new body to maintain the zero tariffs.
"Therefore the United States could fairly argue that fines directed at keeping Boeing aircraft out of the European market break current EU commitments," said one analyst.
